utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, perhaps we could proceed with calling the case first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And this is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Julian Nicholls assisted by case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, Mr. Koumjian. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with my co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For a moment I thought you were waiting for the B/C/S translation. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Slobodan Zecevic, and my dear colleague is Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you too. So let's proceed. There is a preliminary issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: A very brief motion, Your Honour. Ms. Richterova and Ms. Korner asked me to make a motion to request the Court to change the status of the next two witnesses. BT14, which has the disclosure number of 7.139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And BT15, which has the disclosure number of 7.143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They request that they be given closed session, and the reason being that apparently they come from very small hamlets. Most of the persons that they are going to discuss are relatives and their testimony would likely reveal their own identities. If we did it in open session, we'd be going in and out of open session very, very frequently, and we'll just make a request for closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours know that I'm fundamentally opposed to closed sessions. I think courts should operate in the daylight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we agree fully with the position of our learned friend, Mr. John Ackerman, and we oppose the closed session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the first one of these witnesses is due today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We anticipate that the witness would start tomorrow. Actually, Ms. Richterova is doing both, and she is just meeting the second witness this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean the second witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, the -- BT15 she's meeting with right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So BT14 is present --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: BT14 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is present in the The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is in the The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And BT15 is present in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They're both present in The Hague, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically we're talking of BT14 occupying -- starting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's Thursday. Which would mean that BT15, if we finish with BT14 on Thursday, BT15 can testify on Friday. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think the -- Ms. Richterova is estimating -- again, this is just what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking questions is because I was trying to do my best to change the sitting Friday from the afternoon to the morning, but I was told that there may be some difficulty and that the witness wouldn't have arrived in The Hague by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How is it correct if BT14 testifies tomorrow and the next would be BT15, and BT15 is already in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think the -- what I understand is that Ms. Richterova's anticipating that she could finish both tomorrow and that if she can't, then we want to go ahead with the next witness who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is not arriving, as Your Honours said, until Friday afternoon -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So she -- that witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take -- let's take these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is available for Friday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take these issues as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our order is as follows with regard to the Prosecution's motion for the evidence of these two persons to be heard in closed session. We will -- for the time being we are deciding that the first one will be heard in closed session subject to our decision at any moment to decide to revert -- reverse that decision and go into open session if we think that the closed session motion is no longer justified. The same would apply to the second of these witnesses, but we would confirm whether we would proceed with the hearing of his or her evidence, not to give an indication of whether we're talking of a male or a female - when we come to his or her evidence. But for the time being, take it that the motion is being accepted subject to reversal. Okay? And tomorrow we should be also in a position to decide whether we can take advantage of the possibility of having this courtroom available on Friday morning, in which case, if it is at all possible, we'll try to sit on -- in the morning rather than in the afternoon, if it's agreeable with -- with everyone. Because if it's not, then we sit in the afternoon. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Korner has asked for the afternoon because she will only meet the witness Friday morning in order for her to testify in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Five minutes ago you told me that Ms. Richterova is meeting with BT15 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. That's right. I'm talking about the third witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness -- which third witness? The next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe he's protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I think if you really sincerely believe that we will get to the third witness by Friday morning, it will be -- you will be making my day, because it will be the first -- the first time that wishful -- wishful thinking changes into optimism -- a realistic optimism. Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your preference is just that that witness be taken care of even if we have to take him out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. And I'm being reminded that the third witness we had agreed actually on a date for him to be here. But if I remember well, it's not the date -- let me try and find a document that I have. In the meantime, you can bring in the witness, please. Now, my secretary has removed the previous lists because she decided I no longer need them. There is Witness 7.52 -- 7.52. And if I remember well, Ms. Korner had told us that he had requested or there was some kind of prearrangement that he would come on a specified day to give evidence. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The 21st, I believe, which is Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. So that may well be a good reason why we should retain it in the afternoon. Okay. But I frankly don't see how we can finish the other two witnesses between tomorrow -- between today and tomorrow. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour might recall that Witness 7.139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is the next witness, is a witness who we had agreed could be presented by way of 92 bis. And the Talic Defence wanted her brought here for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So we will not have any questions for her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's you. I think Madam Fauveau had not agreed to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, it's -- it's again my recollection -- I may be wrong. But if I remember well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. You're right. I'm just telling you we won't have any questions, so we may in fact be able to finish two witnesses tomorrow. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope your patients in your dental clinic don't have to wait as much as you had to wait again today. Unfortunately again we had some procedural matters to dispose of, which have nothing to do with you. So you don't have to worry about it. But once more I owe you an apology. So let's proceed with the repetition of the solemn declaration that you made yesterday, please. And then we can go ahead with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. And you may sit down. Mr. Nicholls, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yesterday when we left off we were -- we had just finished talking about what happened at the radio -- or at Magarice and how you were going to be taken to the MUP building. Before we get to that, I have one question that I'd like to ask you to clarify some of your testimony yesterday. You talked about the practice of announcing that non-Serbs had to turn in all of their weapons, and you stated that that normally occurred by radio broadcast. That's how you would be informed to turn over weapons. And you gave a personal example of how you heard that broadcast in Sanski Most and turned in your family's hunting rifles. My question is: Do you know which authority made those broadcasts and made those orders, whether that was the civilian local authority or military?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the Sana radio, it was the civilian authorities that made such announcements, in the name of the army because all the weapons that were surrendered were surrendered to the MUP and there was a military department there. The Sanski Most military department was located there too, and that's the part that they would surrender weapons to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's move on now to your transfer to the MUP. And that would have been approximately the 29th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the MUP is in the -- roughly in the -- sorry, did you have a comment?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the centre of the town. On the 27th I was imprisoned and on the 29th - yes, you are right - I was taken to the MUP in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you -- while you were taken to the MUP, were you able to see the condition of Sanski Most town from the car you were transferred in?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was night. There was no electricity. It was in the middle of the night. It was dark. The town wasn't illuminated, so it was impossible to see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What happened upon your arrival at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After midnight --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. My question is: What occurred when you arrived there? What was the first thing that happened to you around midnight when you arrived at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, they put me in the first cell, where I think there were about ten men who had already been arrested. And as they told me later, some of them had been there for two days, some of them had been there for three days. They were colleagues of mine, respected citizens. They'd all been captured in their homes, taken there and put in the first cell in which I was too. The other two who came with me, the other two friends, they were in the other cell, they weren't with me. And there were other people there too, people whom I knew, citizens of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about who was there with you in a few minutes. When you say "they" put you in the first cell, who was they? Who were the guards when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those three soldiers who took me there by car. They took me by the arms and as -- the entrance to MUP, they took me through MUP, through the yard, and then there were cells. They took me there. They unlocked the door and simply put me in one of the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you some photographs now and see if you recognise what's depicted in those photos. So if Denise can help me get the first one to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't very clear. You can't see things very well. It's probably because of the light coming from overhead. So that's why the photograph isn't very clear. You can just make out the contours, the outlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- that's a little bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that's obviously a picture of a hallway. Can you identify what that is a photo of, where that hallway is?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the hallway that we used to enter our cells and to go to the toilets, which was -- which were at the end of this hallway to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there anything in there -- in this photo which is different from the way you remember that hallway in 1992, when you were there?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As -- I can't see it very well, could I have a look at the original and have a look at that? Then I might be able to make things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. If he could be the holder of this copy, not on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right side when we went out into the hallway there were many documents. There was a lot of paper, which we used on a regular basis because we didn't have any other paper. Smokers, when they smoked, then they would gather leaves and they used that paper to roll their cigarettes. I can't see that -- I can't see those documents there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This door, the glass door here didn't exist at the time, I think. Now you can see some kind of a door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could be given the second photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before he's handed the second photo, please, this is going to be tendered as Exhibit number what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P828 would be the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record the witness has been answering questions related to what's being admitted as Exhibit P828.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I speak? The second photograph that you have shown me, that's probably my cell. The door is an iron door and that's -- the door of my cell was like that. The lines were the same, the form is the same. But the beds weren't there. There were just boards which were about 2 metres long and 2 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would very much appreciate if we could really see what the witness is talking about. If there is another copy, the other copy can be put on the ELMO so we really know what -- what the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Although you can barely see anything on the ELMO; at least, I can't -- I can see very little. And probably the dentist is right. It's a question of lighting. Because when they put down the lights, we could see better. Yeah. In fact you can see better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everyone has a right to see -- have a look at the photo while it is being examined by the witness, especially the accused themselves, you know, it's -- in particular. Yes. Sorry to have interrupted you, sir. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This room -- I can now see that there are two beds in it, and they have blankets on them and they are separated. At the time when we were imprisoned, that wasn't there. There were no beds. There were just some sort of boards. There were legs of about 4 or 5 centimetres, and it was a sloping sort of board. It wasn't level. That was the first cell in which I was imprisoned. It didn't have a lock, but a lock would be put on it when they opened the door for us and there was a key down there which was used every time because the lock wasn't very good, it wasn't functioning. Each time we had to get up and push the door from the inside so that it could be unlocked and then the guard could come if he wanted to come. The door was always locked. Sometimes the lock was in that small hole because the room itself was hermetically sealed. The window was 40 by 60 sent metres. It had two sort of locks, two security devices so that you couldn't enter or leave that building. But from the inside there was some tin which covered it and holes had been drilled, about 4 millimetres in diameter. These holes were very small. Between 16 to 20 of us were in that room at times, so there wasn't enough air in that room. It was hot. The weather was hot. There wasn't any water. There wasn't any air. The room was about 2 and a half times 4 or 5 metres. So mostly there was not enough room for us to sit down, let alone to lie down. And in addition you weren't allowed to walk because if they heard that something was happening outside, the police would come immediately to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you need me to say anything -- to add some more information. This room was very small, the weather was very hot. And when we spent the night in there, it was so hot that I -- that water would trickle down the walls, especially on the tin part because of the difference in temperature. So those who were lying down below, they were happy -- they were more content because they weren't lying in water. But those who were not down below, they were wet because of the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point I just want you -- we'll talk about all of those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about all of those living conditions which you're describing. But at this point I just want to get through showing you these photos and having you tell the Chamber any differences between these photos and what you remember your cell being like in 1992. And I think you've described that -- that photo well, that the differences were the door lock and that there were no beds in the room -- or just a board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Nicholls, this will be Exhibit P829.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record. The witness has been answering questions related to document P829.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now if you could be shown the third photo. We'll try to get that on the ELMO as best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document will become Exhibit P830.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my cell. When you look at it from the inside, you can see a radiator in it, which was next to the door, next to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So this would be the view if one's back was to the wall with the window with the metal cover above one's head; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do the dimensions of that cell, as far as you can tell by the door and the size of the radiator, is that the same dimensions that you remember the cell being in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That then is P830. And there's one more photo, Your Honours. The next one will be P831.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you're ready, if you could take a look at that photo. Tell me if you recognise it and describe what it is.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite clear here. You can see that it's a sheet of tin which was used to cover the window, and you can -- it's 40 by 60 centimetres. Those are the dimensions. And you can see the holes which someone had drilled before, the diameter of which was 4 millimetres. And that was our only source of air and of light, since there was no other window. All we had was that metal sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that metal sheet depicted there is the same or very similar to the one you remember being over the window in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was more or less like that. It's probably the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the last photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we've seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That would be P831.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've said that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back and go over a little bit more detail what you started telling us about before we saw cell number 1, which you were kept in. When you arrived and you were placed by the guards in that cell, how many men were in the cell with you the first night?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think seven or eight men were already there. I was brought alone and the other two were taken to another cell. I don't know how many people were in other cells, but there were seven to eight in mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On that first day or night, rather, that you arrived, were you beaten or mistreated upon your arrival at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came there, I'd already been beaten up and I was nearly comatose, and the only thing that was important to me at the time was that when they saw how I looked when I got there they gave me some space to lie down. So I had a privilege of being able to lie on this board and the rest had to sit. When they saw my back and when they saw what condition I was in, this is how they treated me, so that I could lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know the men who were in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who were they? What kind of people were they? Where did you know them from?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from Sanski Most, distinguished citizens, educated people, businessmen, people who were well off. Not all of them were active in political parties. There were those of us who were, but there were also those that did not belong to any parties. And there was a man there of Catholic faith whom I didn't know before. He was a bank director and then he was fired and taken immediately to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were -- and correct me if I'm wrong, but you stayed in that cell number 1 for about three months, about 95 days.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 95 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said there were seven men in that cell the night you arrived. What was -- did that number stay constant, or what was the greatest number of men that were kept in that cell with you at any point during those 95 days?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually almost daily people were brought in, interrogated, and then most likely taken to Krings or sports hall or Betonirka or to the school, because there was more room there, and those people that had been interrogated were not returned to our cell any more. Some people stayed for several days. Some people stayed for longer. But the five of us were there in the same cell from the very first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you remember the names, who were the five of you that you're -- that you're speaking of?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was myself, Faik Biscevic, Redzo Kurbegovic, Sabic Suad, Batic Zikrija and Faruk Botonjic. I was a dentist. Redzo was a civil engineer. Sabic Suad was a public prosecutor. Mr. Batic and Mr. Botonjic were professionals in the MUP. They were policemen and had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just trying to be clear on -- what was the greatest amount of men -- I understand people were coming in and out, that it was somewhat transitory. But what were the greatest amount of people who were kept in that cell, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion there were 20 of us there. So we simply were one on top of the other, because this room had 8 or 9 square metres and could not hold 20 people in it. People that were brought there had all been beaten. And since all of these people were beaten up, they didn't really care if they just had to stand on one leg or they could sit down. They were simply happy to be in a room where they didn't beat them. They were simply happy not to be tortured any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, was any medical care provided to these men who you say had been beaten or to yourself while you were there? Was anybody treated by a doctor while there were there, any of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only used batons there. Nobody received any medical treatment. I, as much as I was able, tried to help. In the beginning the men who was a nurse, in his room tried to help, but he soon went elsewhere. He was the nurse, so he helped people in the second cell and I helped in the first one. We had to do everything we could with our five fingers and the water that we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me about what kind of toilet facilities or -- and shower facilities you were allowed while you were in there for those three months.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came into the prison, to the cells, the first thing they ordered to me and Redzo Kurbegovic was to clean two toilets that were at the end, behind those three cells. I assumed that they'd been using those toilets. Perhaps they'd been used by some prisoners. I don't know. But the toilets were blocked and there was perhaps half a metre of faeces and paper in that -- in those two toilets. It was difficult to open the door and get into the toilet. And they forced us to clean it with our bare hands and to clean the water pipe -- sewage pipe so that the toilets could be used. This is what we had to do in the first days, and we were actually happy that we'd been allowed to do that so that we could be able to use the toilets at all. In the morning they would give us five minutes at breakfast time to use toilets and then also five minutes in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's pretty clear from those photos there were no toilet facilities or running water available for you inside the cell; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing in the cells. There was a small wash basin and a small faucet in front, but the water system that we had assumed that there had to be a water pump that would work on electricity and pump the water. So since the pump wasn't working, that meant that we weren't able to use this wash basin and faucet at all; almost never at all. In the room in which we were, there was nothing else. They only opened the room five minutes in the morning and five minutes in the evening so that we could go out to eat breakfast and dinner and use toilets. In the meantime, we got by, by using juice containers, 1-litre juice containers. And prior to -- and we also used our underwear, undershirts and shirts, because a lot of people had diarrhoea, so they basically used their clothing and towels as toilets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And tell me about whether or how often you were able to shower and wash yourself and bathe under these conditions.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went for -- I and everybody else went for 62 days without changing our underwear or clothing. And on the sixty-second day, a Serb guard, whom, as I learned, was an agriculture engineer, he came one morning, opened the cell -- because he normally brought the food. And he lined us up, took another soldier to escort us, and we went through the yard and there was a football field on the other side of the prison, and there were shower stalls there for football players. And on the sixty-second day we were allowed to go there, to take three minutes to wash ourself and wash our clothing, which we were very happy to do, just using our hands, without any soap. And then we went back with wet clothes but very happy that we were able to take any kind of a shower after 62 days. And then once again, during those 95 days of imprisonment, we were again taken by him to take a shower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How were you able to keep track of the days while you were in there? How do you know that was the sixty-second day?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tin that we had on the window, as I told you, had holes in it. So during the first ten days we hoped that we would be released. But then after that we started counting among ourselves whether it was the ninth or the tenth day. And then I had an idea to take a sheet of paper and to start filling the holes in the tin or -- so we would move this little piece of paper in a different hole every day. And this is how we were able to count the days, using these holes that were in the tin. And I would like to add something else. Since there were that many of us, in the beginning especially, both in the first and in the second and the third cells, it was very difficult to use toilets, because they would tell us the first cell has three minutes to use the toilets and have breakfast. So we basically had to run. And then one guard came and took out two men from our cell and took them behind the place where we ate. Behind there, there was a room behind which there was about a metre and a half of space in between there and Betonirka building. And he ordered them to dig a hole 1 metre wide. And they put two boards there. And this is -- was a makeshift toilet that we used, because the other toilet was very crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in this small space with that many men in it, how were you able to sleep at night? How -- what were the sleeping arrangements?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no sleeping there. During the day and otherwise too we simply sat there quiet. We were -- we had to sit tightly with our legs very close to our bodies, next to each other, and nap if we could within 24 hours. Some people slept during the day. Some people slept during the night. But it wasn't typical sleeping like people normally sleep. This was just making by in the sitting position. So when we came to Manjaca after 95 days, we were completely almost disabled. I had lost 32 kilos during those 95 days, and we were simply happy to be able to stretch out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So other than leaving to go to the toilet or that time you were allowed to go take a shower, you weren't let out to get any exercise or walk around at any point during your stay there to stretch your legs.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if the guard called one of us out. Since the troops were there, the troops ate in the canteen. We were usually taken to the canteen to clean it up. So that was the only possibility to get some exercise. Other than that, no, we never left the cell; not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to move on. If you could tell me what the air quality was like in that cell and what the temperature was like during those summer months in Sanski Most when you were held there.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were imprisoned at the end of May. And on August 27th we left that place. In Bosnia June, July, and August are summer months with real summer heat. The temperature is normally above 30 centigrade, so it is very stuffy and humid. It rains very infrequently. So these cells in which we were really -- had a terrible stench, so that in the morning when the guard would come to open this cell they usually had to hold a handkerchief over their nose. And then while we were eating the door would stay open for three to five minutes and that was really a lucky circumstance because that was the only time when the room got any extra air. And then the rest of the time we were locked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And typically -- if you briefly describe -- you said the food. What kind of food were you given on a typical day while you were there, in the morning and in the evening?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning -- in the beginning when the war just broke out and when they brought us there the troops -- the soldiers ate there, so there was more food and there were more remains, leftovers left to us after the troops. And then afterwards it became -- it became a standard practice that bread would be split into many pieces and each of us would get one slice of bread and -- and a cup of some -- something to drink. And the size of the slice depended on how many people there were there and into how many pieces the loaf was sliced. And for our second meal, we would get whatever was left over and again a slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You say you lost approximately 30 kilos while you were held there, you believe.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 32 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During the time when you were in the cell, were you and these prisoners who you knew from Sanski Most, were you allowed to talk amongst yourselves? Were you allowed to do anything to pass the time?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went to the toilet we saw this window which was on that side, and we would pass by it and we could see that there was always a chair under the window and there was somebody always there standing and listening to what we were saying. So if we had any conversation among us, then we would speak very quietly so that nothing could be heard. And if -- on one occasion they brought in their own soldiers, Serb, who detonated a bomb, and he was quite crude. He was banging on the door asking to be released and they beat him as long as he was still speaking and talking. So we didn't even dare speak or make any noise because they could come in and beat us and do anything they wanted to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me -- and we'll move on. When was the first -- you weren't beaten on the day you arrived, on the night you arrived. When was the first time that you were personally beaten in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already came in all beaten up, I had blood in my urine and I wasn't really doing well and I wasn't beaten in the first few days. There was -- neither were others. We were simply there in prison. They fed us and so on. On the 9th of June, they called me, Kurbegovic, Ferid Burnic, Hase Osmancevic. They took us up there to the MUP building. I was taken upstairs to the room -- I think number 32. And I got there at 11.00 and stayed until 6.00 p.m. They interrogated me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can briefly describe what you mean by they interrogated you and what happened to you in that room.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got into that room, next to the door there was a chair and they told me to sit down there. Well, the door was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, instead of saying "they," if you know who the persons were, if you can identify them by name, then please go ahead and -- so that we will avoid a further question later on. Thank you. How many of them, whether you know them by name, whether they were policeman or whether they were -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on this occasion there were all professional officers whom I knew personally. They used to work in MUP. They used to be investigators in peacetime. Dosenovic Mima was the chief investigator. Stojnovic -- I think his first name was Darinko. He was the note-taker. He sat across the table. Rajkica Stanic was a judge in Sanski Most. And since the Serbs took over power, he put on a military uniform and acted as a coordinator taking documents from one room to the other and coordinating their work. And there were also two soldiers whose names I don't know who used to beat people. The usual practice was to have Mima begin interrogation. I had to sit on the chair. I wasn't allowed to move or get up. He interrogated and also beat people with his hands and kicked them. Once he got tired, which was after about an hour and a half, he would leave the room and then in the meantime Rajkica would come in and they would talk among themselves. So when Mima got tired, then after that two soldiers would come in with batons. And they didn't interrogate us or say anything. They simply beat us. In the beginning when I was there Mirzet Karabeg and Burnic Ferid were brought in as well. They were facing the wall. They were not allowed to look at me nor I at them and they asked them to confirm something for which they were accusing me. They naturally confirmed everything they were asked to confirm. And after that they left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you were beaten by both civilian police officers who had been civilian police officers before this conflict and also by soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took turns, policemen, officers, and upon their leaving the room two soldiers would come in who did not interrogate us, just beat us. And then once the soldiers would leave, then Mima would come in again continue interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And briefly what types of questions would they ask you? You said they asked your -- people you knew to confirm what was said about you. What were they trying -- these interrogators, what were they trying to get you to confess to, or what information were they trying to get from you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted me to confess that I was guilty for everything that was going on, that it was all my fault. They wanted me to confess that I'd been arming Muslims in Muslim places. They wanted me to admit that I had weapons. Since I denied all that then Mima, who interrogated me -- he cursed my balija mother and he told me, "Well, everybody is accusing you but according to you you are blameless." And then he had five bullets of different calibres and he asked me which bullet do you want me to use to kill you? And I told him, "Well, use the largest bullet." And then in the end a -- there was a photographer from whom I borrowed money and failed to return on time. Then this photographer talked in cafes that I failed to return money, and I guess that one of the informants of Mima sat in those cafes and then Mima told me, "Well, it is said here that you borrowed money from people." And I said, "Well, call that man here and have him say that I borrowed money in order to buy weapons." This is simply all he wanted. And once he got tired, he would leave and then the soldiers would come in and if they were not happy with the amount of beating I received, then they would take my legs and put them under the chair so that I couldn't move and then they would beat me all over my body, over my soles, so that I couldn't walk for 20 days. And I think that I had blood in my urine for more than a month, because I was beaten all over. I was beaten from 11.00 until 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How often -- you've just described a terrible beating. How often -- how many times approximately do you think you were beaten during your imprisonment at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day we finished this at 6.00 p.m. and he said, "We'll continue our conversation the following day." However, strangely enough when I got there the following day, he didn't beat me at all. He asked me to sign a document, which I signed without reading it. And then after that, I never really received a beating as bad as the one on the first day, because on that first interrogation they wanted simply to break me down, to have me sign everything they wanted me to sign, and we did as we were told because that was the easiest thing to do. And then after that, since in our cell only us civic leaders remained - there were five of us in the first cell, six in the second, and three in the third cell - we received what they called special treatment and heads of shifts would guard us in -- for eight hours. And this special treatment basically boiled down to the fact that nobody else was allowed into our cells except them. And these premises were in the area where there were constantly troops and policemen. So troops would come in at any time, they would shoot if they wanted to, simply do what they wanted. So sometimes if a guard wanted, he could after business hours, after 2.00 p.m., turn over the keys of our cells to soldiers so that soldiers could come in and do as they pleased. And that took place every day, despite the fact that we were as they said people that deserved special treatment. Anybody could come in and beat us if they so pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were you ever formally charged with any criminal offence during this time?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they threatened to accuse us and said that the Muslims and Croats would put us on trial. Then they said that we would be going -- to be taken to an official court, that we'd be officially tried. But up till Manjaca nothing of that kind happened. We weren't tried, but we were taken to Manjaca. Our other leaders who were killed in the night -- well, yes, I heard that there was some sort of a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you meet any Red Cross representative while you were in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July the guard came, the one who locked up. He told us to open the door and to take out the things that we had in there and he said that we shouldn't close the door -- that we shouldn't return, that we should stay in the yard and sit down there, to sweep up the rooms, to clean -- to tidy things up, to put things in order. We were surprised by this. First of all, we were surprised because for the first day -- for the first time on that day we had the opportunity of seeing each other, all the people who were in the cells, because the principle was that we would go out, eat quickly, drink quickly, and then we would return. The door to our cell would be looked and then the door to another cell would be open so that people couldn't see each other and prevent us from arranging anything. That was the first time we were all allowed to go out into the yard and perhaps we sat out there for about a -- we'd been sitting there for about an hour when a Red Cross representative appeared. I think he was from France. And he was accompanied by an interpreter. He came and he brought registers in which he entered our names, said that we had been registered with the Red Cross. He gave us the possibility of contacting our families. We were provided with a little sheet of paper where we could write down a message up to ten words, and with each of us in the cell -- he spoke to each person, everyone from the cell, and he asked us where we were from, how we had got there, what we were guilty of. So we were all able to speak for about 30 seconds or a minute with this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did conditions improve after that visit for you at all?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. When he went, everything remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at any point were you allowed any visits from any friends, family members, or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, perhaps towards the end of July and August, they allowed us this because they said that there was not so much food for the soldiers, since we almost had nothing for -- for lunch. So they allowed us on Saturday to have visits in the morning. So since I didn't have anyone, apart from a cousin and a girlfriend of my son, they came to visit me on Saturday. That was a few Saturdays before we were taken away to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before we moved on -- before we move on, was anybody specifically singled out that you observed for more severe beatings or more frequent beatings? Was anybody singled out for extra punishment?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said -- and I'll repeat this. From the 25th to the 27th all the party leaders, they'd been brought from their houses, from their homes, and locked up in the cells. The only person they didn't lock up was the party secretary, Kamber. And the hodzas, Seferovic Emir -- Emir Seferovic, I think that a month and a half later one morning when we got up and went to breakfast Suad Sabic's leather jacket was in the yard. He said that it seems if they have captured Hasib. And that was true and a few days later they brought in Emir Seferovic. And in the case of Hasib and Emir Seferovic, as they were clerics -- as he was a cleric, on every day -- every day after a meal there were regular beatings. And when night fell, every night -- in addition to us, to beating us, they had probably beaten us sufficiently so they didn't have any desire to carry on. But every night they beat them, but not just every night but also in the morning since the two of them were alone in a cell they would take them out separately to eat and then when they returned them, four or five of them would put them into the cell and then you would hear the screaming, the groaning, and then they would laugh, they would talk about what they had done to them, how they had beaten them. This took place on a regular basis, these two prisoners were beaten every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've used the name Kamber and also Hasib. But that's the same person. It's Hasib Kamber; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasib Kamber is one person, the secretary. And Emir Seferovic is another person. And if I can add something, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that as they were soldiers, these soldiers would go to the front, as they said. Usually a new shift would last. A shift would last for 20 or 25 days. After 25 days, a return from a -- return from the front would be organised. And after they would -- after returning from the front, they would all go to the playground which was next to the place we were kept in. This is where they would be lined up, and Mr. Basara would give a speech. This never failed to happen. I don't know whether Talic -- Mr. Talic came; I can't say. But officers came and they encouraged their soldiers, and it was particularly difficult then because they would shoot and there were no limits. And once the officers had given their speeches -- made their speeches, they would leave the playground. Men would leave there -- would remain there. They would get drunk. They would go into the yard of the prison. They would get the key from the duty guard who was there and then they could go whatever they wanted to do and do this for as long as they wanted to do. And this was something that happened regularly when these soldiers would return from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just last question on this. If you know, who was the person in charge of the MUP? Who was running the MUP at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first few days? Are you talk about the first few days? Dobri -- Drago Vrucinic was the head of the MUP for us in these three cells and which Mico Krunic was the head for Betonirka. And I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you leave the MUP? When were you taken out of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the translation -- I'm asking you -- you arrived at the MUP around the 28th or 29th of May. I'm asking when you left the MUP after that 95 days that you stayed there, you said. Do you remember the date when you were transferred out of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 65 days. We were there for 95 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you were released -- after that 95 days, where did you go? What happened?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As would happen every morning, we went to have breakfast. We went to the toilets. And then we returned to the cell. About 11.00 we heard that the guards were talking about something. You could hear that in the yard. The doors to our cells were opened. The duty guard appeared and said, "Gather your things and go out." The same thing happened in the other cells. But we heard Kamber and Seferovic saying, "You stay on. You're not going. The others are going." When we got out, they lined us up and we saw that there was a bus that had arrived in the yard and it was waiting there. The door was open and they said, "Get in the bus."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know when we break, Your Honour. But it might not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's convenient for you to break now -- to stop now, we'll stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would prefer that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have another five minutes. But if we stop now, obviously we will start five minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a break now of 15 minutes, doing our best to resume at five minutes to 4.00, if that's okay. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We were just about to start talking about your transfer to Manjaca camp. And that would have been in late August 1992. And you were just telling us about how you were told to go outside and you lined up and there was a bus. If you could continue now. Tell me where you went on that bus that morning.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got into the bus. Another policeman was waiting for us there and he said, "Sit down. No one is to get on or get off. You're going to be taken away now. Nothing nasty will happen to you." We left the prison yard and went down a street. There is a way through Sanski Most which leads to Bosanska Krupa. We took this road. We thought we were going to be exchanged because the border was there -- or rather, demarcation line between the army and the Serbian positions. But we didn't go towards Krupa, but there was an area where there was a factory called Krings. The bus went there. And then these people of ours who were in the Krings Hall also started getting on the bus. About 45 to 50 people were in the bus. That's how many got out of the Krings Hall. And then we headed back in the direction of the prison. We didn't get to the prison but we passed by the prison and took this byway, this round about way and headed in the direction of Kljuc. And then we also thought that we would be exchanged or would be going to some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Thank you. When you say that at Krings you -- there were -- more people got on the bus who were "these people of ours," who are you referring to? Who got on the bus at Krings?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we recognised a lot of people. They were Muslims and Croats. As we were told later on, they were in -- in this Krings factory. They got on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were these civilians to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue. I'm sorry. You said you were heading back towards the prison. You were hoping that you were going to be exchanged. You did not actually reach the MUP. Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We headed towards Kljuc. And when we got to the village of Vrhpolje, that's by the River Sana where the bridge is -- there's a crossroads on the left and there is a macadam road. I'm a hunter, so I know that area very well. And I noticed we were going -- I noticed the mountain Mulez -- which is called -- and the Serbian village of Oljace is behind the mountain. And behind that village Manjaca is located. So we were a hundred per cent sure that we were going to Manjaca. And that proved to be the case. We were taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And approximately how many civilians were transported with you to Manjaca that day? I'm trying to get an idea of how many people were in this transfer that you're telling us about.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, up to about 50. Since there are 40 seats in the bus and the people on the bus, the number was slightly higher, and it was probably up to 50 people. We didn't count everyone, but that should be the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, was everybody who had been with you in cell number 1 in the MUP that day transferred to Manjaca along with you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Manjaca camp? Who met you and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of the Manjaca camp, we were ordered to get out and to line up four by four and to stand before the entrance to Manjaca. And from -- on the other side we saw that there were people who had been lined up, and they were looking outside. We didn't know what was happening at the time. But later on we found out that the old people and children who were in Manjaca, a bus came to collect them and took them back to Sanski Most. When they opened the entrance to that camp, we entered the campgrounds. They told us to sit down on the grass and to wait for orders and told us not to talk, et cetera. There was perhaps some sort of a warehouse there, something that used to be a warehouse, and they told us to enter one by one. Up to ten people could enter the area at a time. And then they stripped us and they told us to display the things -- the items that we had. And I said during the last few Saturdays we had visits and our relatives would bring us clothes to change into and they would bring blankets for some people. They brought me a brush which was specific. It consisted of two parts, and it was easy to carry, maybe a toothbrush. When we stripped we had to turn to face the wall. And on the other side, the Sarenci, the guards who were wearing sort of camouflage uniforms, they looked at the items and took what they wanted. They made a list of our names. They said, "You're going to camp number 2, stable number 5." And since there were about 50 of us and that was a big stable, we all went to that second camp. When they had registered us, they lined us up. And as that was in the first camp -- those were the grounds of the first camp, they took us to the second camp then and they showed us the stables. We entered the stables, and each man tried to find a place for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that there were soldiers in the camp and you also used the words "they" a few times when you were talk about who ordered you to do certain things upon your arrival. Once you were inside the camp, were all the guards and the personnel running the camp soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we left the prison -- the Sanski prison, then official policemen turned up, wearing uniforms and the policeman who was guarding us, who was sitting on the first seat, they were in different uniforms, in blue uniforms. Later on we found out that these policemen who worked as civilian policemen, they had no access to the camp. The people in camouflage uniforms were there. They were soldiers from the JNA, and they had access to the camp. And beyond the fence, that's where the policemen wearing blue uniforms could stand guard. So there was an obvious difference between these two police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say you were assigned to stable number 5 and that the men would go in there and then try to find a place, a spot for themselves. Can you describe the interior -- or what that structure was like, the stable you were kept in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have a photo or anything to show him, then we can speed it up. That way you have our authority to proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to have him describe it from his memory, Your Honour, rather than use a photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you prefer, we can probably find one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've seen several, actually. We've seen video clips. Anyway, please go ahead, Mr. Biscevic. Can you recall -- recount to us what it was like in the stable that you were in, in Manjaca. Can you describe the place to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a huge area, about 80 metres along and 20 metres wide. In the middle there was a sort of elevated part which was concrete -- made of concrete, about 5 or 6 metres wide. There were metal bars on the sides to prevent cattle from climbing up. There were doors on each side so that tractors could enter with a trailer and so that the cattle could be provided with food. On the left and right side, a little lower down, 1 metre lower down, there was also a part where we inmates on the upper surface -- detainees would lie on the upper surface on both sides and on the lower surface there were detainees on both sides, two rows of detainees, and their heads were facing towards the outside and their legs towards the inside. There was no ceiling, just a roof. So there was enough air because this -- this area hadn't been hermetically sealed off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you stated when you were describing the MUP how because of the confinement you had trouble walking and there was terrible air in cell number 1. Were you saying is it in some ways when you arrived at Manjaca, those conditions were better; is that correct? You had more air and you could move around better?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And another thing which was better for us who had come there from the cells -- we had enough air. That's what was important. We saw that there was no ceiling, there was enough air, so you could breathe as much as you wanted to, you could breathe freely. And thirdly, as there were a lot of people there, then at breakfast time and for dinner you'd go to the toilet. And we could also go outside and be in the sun for a couple of hours, and that was a vast improvement when compared to the conditions in the -- in the cell. That's why I said that the conditions were better there than in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were in Manjaca from the end of August until your release on November 15th. During that time you were there, did the conditions stay the same, get better, or get worse over those months?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived there the older inmates in Manjaca said that the situation was excellent in comparison to what it used to be before, and they said that an international inspection team had come and entered the camp. And after that, the situation improved; things got a lot better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you meet anybody from the Red Cross or other international humanitarian organisations while you were in Manjaca? I'm speaking of you personally.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was a medical expert and someone from the Red Cross came every day, a medical official, and he would control -- inspect the food, since the inmates were so emaciated. They were unable to walk. So initially when I first arrived there, they would distribute milk and oil, to which sugar had been added. They would give the inmates who were not able to walk this, and this nurse came every day -- this medical worker and ensured that this was distributed. And the cooks preparing the food were people I knew from Sanski Most. And when we spoke, they said, "This is a colleague of yours. He's a medical -- he has a medical background." And so we spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You started talking about food. Can you describe what type of food and how much you would be given typically during a day in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got there, they told me then that the food was excellent. For breakfast we got a quarter of bread, we got milk, tea, or cocoa. We'd get a cup of milk, tea, or cocoa. And when we had arrived -- when we arrived there they distributed tins for two inmates. That was for breakfast. And for lunch you would get a cooked meal and also a quarter of bread -- a quarter of a loaf of bread. The difference was that a certain amount of food would be cooked. And those who first turned up, they would be given this food first. They would get a sort of -- food of a better quality. It would be thicker. And then those who came later, as there was not very much food, in order to ensure that there was enough food, the cooks would take a bucket of water and pour it in so as to have more food. And then you would get a lot of water as food. Perhaps you'd have a few beans or some lentils in this liquid. And sometimes you would turn up and you wouldn't get anything other than a slice of bread. That was lunch. There was no dinner. That was what we would get for lunch and dinner. I would also like to add -- to point out that when I was there, that was towards the end. Merhamet started sending meat on Wednesday at times, and we could see that -- the inmates and I could see that because they would bring that meat inside, and this was provided as aid for the inmates. The following day, when there was food made out of this meat, there was almost nothing left. Perhaps a lucky person would get a piece of meat or so because the cooks said that the soldiers who were on guard, they would take this meet away, they would take it to their homes. So we got very little of this meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So on any given day one prisoner might get an adequate amount of food, another might get only water, depending on when they were allowed to eat lunch; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never enough food. You'd get a plate. But no one would ask you whether the food you had on the plate was sufficient or not you had to be happy with what you got. But if you turned up first you'd get a thick broth that was good. If you came later on, then the broth you would get would be thinner and you wouldn't fare as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, is what you're saying is that even if you arrived first and got the thick broth, it would be better, but that it wasn't enough, that it wasn't sufficient?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'd always get a plate of food and a quarter of a loaf of bread. That's what you would get. There was no lunch and there was no dinner. This was something that you'd get between lunch and dinner. That's what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What was the quality of the water which you were given to drink in Manjaca, and can you describe how that was given to you.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a big problem in Manjaca because there wasn't any water, so there wasn't enough water and there wasn't enough drinking water and the water that we had was a very poor quality. As the water was a problem, when representatives of the Red Cross arrived we asked them for us to be allowed to have water so that we could drink enough water -- have enough water to drink. Then the Red Cross sent plastic canisters, 4-litre canisters. They are made of plastic. And one canister would be given to five inmates. And about 2 or 3 kilometres from the camp there was a lake where cattle would go to drink -- would be taken to drink. And every day about 100, 200, or 300 inmates would go with those canisters and they would fill these canisters up, since that water was dirty and it wasn't suitable for use, for -- when I was there, I started filling up a canister with water and the policeman who took us there, he started urinating where I was getting water. They were just looking for an excuse to beat you up. So that's how they would gather water and then people had diarrhoea on a daily basis. Most inmates had stomach problems, stomach illnesses, and we complained about this and later on the Red Cross brought us tablets which were put in those canisters. They were tablets for disinfection. So that improved the water to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said that inmates would get ill from drinking this bad water. Can you tell me what medical care was provided for sick inmates in Manjaca to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually -- when I got there, the condition was already improved. So when I got there a nurse would come into the barracks and ask who was sick and then those names would be recorded, and then there was a physician there, Dr. Sabanovic, and another person, Mehmed something. And they would see patients and give what medical treatment they were able to do so. I, as a person with medical background, would give advice or any other help that I could to people who had different kinds of wounds. And people would also go and see these physicians and the physicians would be -- would provide what first aid they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you work as a dentist while you were in Manjaca? Did you do anything in your own personal expertise?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to Manjaca, there was a dentist there, Flat Leopold, a colleague of mine from Kljuc. His father was a German and was imprisoned as well as a soldier of the army. And since this dentist's father was a German, I guess he had connections and he was released soon after my arrival. For a long time there was no dentist there at all. Asim, the nurse that I mentioned, since there were 3.000 inmates there, that means that there would always be at least somebody who had some dental problems. Then he, Asim, would extract teeth and sometimes he would frequently break their teeth. And if that should happen, they would bring a patient to me. And if I was able, I would help the person. And since this is really -- this really was not a proper way to fix these problems, then I guess somebody told the guards that I had been a dentist and then they came and told me that I could treat people in the same room in which Dr. Mehmed and Sabanovic saw patients together with a nurse. So it was a small room, a former warehouse; perhaps 4 by 4 metres. In one corner I had a chair and I also had some -- I had pliers and when a patient would come towards the end of my stay there the Red Cross used to provide us some anaesthetics, Novocaine, and if I could I would anaesthetise the patient and pull out their teeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have enough anaesthetic for what you considered an adequate amount for the patients you -- the people you were seeing?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not nearly enough. People most often went without any anaesthetic. And at any rate, we were never able to provide a full dose to anyone because we only got one bottle and we didn't dare ask for another one. If they brought us one, then fine. But if they didn't, then we couldn't ask for any. So I would give a bit more than the regular -- I would give a bit less than the regular dose. And some people even had to go without anaesthetics. On some occasion if teeth broke, which happened often because the pliers were not good and the patients were quite young, then in that case I had to make a much bigger wound and in fact damage the tooth bone, because that was the only way to extract the tooth. Because if the tooth remained in, then the patient would suffer terrible pain. So I had to do what I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said some of the people you treated were quite young. And earlier on you said when you arrived that a bus was leaving with old men and you said children, I believe. Can you describe the range of ages of people that you saw in Manjaca while you were there, the youngest people you saw and the oldest.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were children. And I considered children those who are 16 or 17 years old. There were many of them, and there was even a greater number of the elderly. So it wasn't unusual to see a 70-year-old man whom they considered to have been a soldier and a dangerous person. There were children there, malnourished. There were retarded children with whom we had problems, and they were considered to have been soldiers as well. So there were all kinds of people there. When the first bus left, not all of the children boarded it. And those that remained left on November 15th together with us, the elderly. So those who were younger than 18 left with the elderly persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you personally know or recognise from Sanski Most anybody under 18 who was in the camp, any 16-, 17-year-olds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After his arrival?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is, from the end of August till November, when you left Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were two boys whom I knew personally, Kalic Senad and Sabic. I don't know his first name. He was the son of my colleague, Sabic -- or rather, his sister. And I knew him a bit more than the others, as well as Kalic Senad who was retarded and who used to live close to my house. So I knew him, and he was in my stable and there were children in other stables too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said these people were considered soldiers. Were any of these people you knew -- were these people that were in there with you soldiers, or can you describe the people that you knew personally who were in there at the same time that you were? I'm talk about your personal experience, not anything that you learned later.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the people whom I knew were civilians, and I can guarantee this. Absolutely. I knew them personally. I knew where they'd been brought from. I knew what they were accused of, and I know that that wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, during your time in Manjaca, were you personally beaten or physically abused by the guards?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those older ones who were in the camp used to tell us that it was the usual norm to have the inmates taken out and beaten. Once we got there, it wasn't so. And at night when the stables were locked, it was quiet. Around Manjaca, around our camp, on the outside of the wire there were people with dogs, the guards with dogs who stood every 5 or 6 metres guarding the perimeter so that nobody could go out. In the evening, at night after it got dark, these dogs would howl, and it was unpleasant to listen to. And the older inmates told me that strangely enough in the past when they used to beat inmates, the dogs howled too, together with people, the whole time while they were beaten. And this always took place at the same time. So it was quite weird that the dogs continued to howl even though there was no more beating going on. When I was there, the beating was not typical, was not usual, of the kind that used to take place before. Sometimes they would beat those people who were talking, because stables would be locked at 5.00 and then after 5.00 it had to be absolutely quiet. And in one stable there were five or six hundred people, so it couldn't be completely quiet. And if they found that one stable was a bit more loud than they wanted it to be, then there was always a person in every stable who was in charge of the stable, who was sort of the head of it. And in our stable that position was held by the man called Boskovic. There was a guard there called Sarenac.
