And for example if one stable was a bit more loud than they thought was normal, then the head of the stable would be told to take out ten people and those ten would be beaten, and the head of the stable had to select who would be taken out. Or another example: Sometimes in the kitchen, there would be a lot of us there and they were all -- some people were retarded, some people were simply with poor nerves. And if we were more loud than acceptable to them, then Sarenac would call the person who was more loud out and that person would have to put his arms on his back and bend his head and then Sarenac would beat him. And if the person fell down, he would have to get up and regain the same position and Sarenac would continue to beat him. If he complained or even tried to protect himself by raising his hand or arm, then two more guards would come in and then they would take that person to the place that we called the white yard, and that was a place where they beat people. There was a room for beating. And this was a daily occurrence. Yes, it was beating, but it wasn't as bad as it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to be clear, my question was also whether you were personally beaten. Were you ever punched or kicked or beaten while you were in Manjaca at all? I'm just speaking personally about you yourself, not what you observed with other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tell us yes or no. Just yes or no, please. If you were beaten, tell us. And if you were not, then tell us that you were not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said no. You weren't beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. It's not perfectly clear to me. You were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He wasn't beaten. This is what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. On one occasion they did beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you said that at 5.00 everybody had to be quiet and the stables would be shut down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to get a quick picture. When would the day start? What time would you -- would the day start for you when you were in there?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day would also begin at 5.00 a.m. These troops would come into the camp and yell. As soon as they yelled, we all had to jump up, and no one was allowed to continue lying down. Since the toilets were outside of the stables, we would normally line up and then ten by ten inmates would go to the toilet. And when they came back, the other ten would go. So this started at 5.00 a.m. After that, we had breakfast. And then again one stable would go first and then the next one and so on. We would all line up. And that continued until some 3.00. And then we would go back into the stables. And since most of the inmates went out to work, then they would also select those who would go out to work and those who would remain in the camp. So there was activity going on all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's talk about how you came to be released from Manjaca. Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On November 15th all of those who were above 50 and those who were younger than 18 were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what happened? Tell me how you were released and where you went.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six days prior to release -- and even before that it was rumoured that we would be released because the Red Cross was looking for a third country that would take us in. So some five or six days before the release, they told me to go to a room where supposedly an officer wanted to talk to me. So I went there, and he talked to me, and he said since I was older than 50, I would be released on November 15th. He said it had been decided that those who were above 50 and those younger than 18 should be released. And since I satisfied the requirements, he told me I would be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then you were released and you went on a bus convoy, I believe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where did you go? Where were you released to? Where was the end destination after you got out of Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a holding centre in Karlovac in Croatia, and all of us went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, before we finish, I want to go back -- you've talked about what happened to you after May 27th when you were arrested all the way up through November. And I just want to talk a little bit about what happened to your property and to the other members of your family. At the time in May 1992 - correct me if I'm wrong - but you owned two -- your home in Sanski Most, two dentist practices, a goldsmith shop, a holiday home or cabin nearby in Sanski Most, and a sort of farm. What happened to that property? I don't need to know in a lot of detail, but was any of that property intact when you returned in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was looted and destroyed. I didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what had happened to your home, how it had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day I was taken away, at 1.00 they came to get my wife and my children at 4.00, and not only them. They went door to door and took people out. Men were separated from women. So my house was deserted that same day I was arrested. A neighbour remained there by accident and saw that a truck came in with a trailer, and she saw the soldiers carry out the equipment in my dental practice and all other valuable things. She heard that they threw a grenade on my house so that everything was destroyed. I had a Mercedes which was of a great interest to officers and soldiers. And in addition to that, they took everything else of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In short, all of your property was taken or destroyed after you were arrested in May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was looted and destroyed. So I didn't find anything intact. Everything was ruined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that the morning that you were arrested your son Haris during a lull in the shelling set off to take his girlfriend home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell me what happened to Haris, your son, after that, please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the shelling started again at 11.00, he hadn't come back by then. I was taken away at 1.00 and then my two other sons, Nedim and Edin together with my wife, were evicted from the house. Since Haris was at his girlfriend's house, he was taken away from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was he taken to the sports hall? Is that your understanding -- in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was taken to the sports hall. But shortly thereafter he was taken to the high school in Kljucka Ulica, where there was also a gym there. I think he also spent two days in Betonirka. And then on the 6th of June he was taken to Manjaca in the first group that went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened to your son Haris Biscevic on the 6th of June when he went to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first group of inmates was taken to Manjaca then. As they came out of the vehicle, the soldiers would beat them. In the meantime, six people's names were called out, and they were told to go back into a truck. My son Haris Biscevic was among those six. They boarded them into a truck, beaten up as they were, and they drove them somewhere and we haven't had any information to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, your other two sons, Edin and Nedim are twins. They're twins.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just tell me briefly what you know. What happened to the twins on that same day that you were arrested in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested at 1.00. They were taken away at 4.00 together with my wife. My wife was told to go to one side, and they, the boys, were taken to the sports hall together with all the men from our neighbourhood. They remained in the sports hall. And then on the 6th of June, the day Haris was taken away, one of the twins was taken away as well, Nedim, whereas Edin remained in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you know what became of Edin, who was -- who stayed in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Edin, who remained in the sports hall, stayed there until July 7th and then the camp in the sports hall was closed down, so that all of those who were in the Krings factory, in Betonirka, and in the sports hall were loaded into trucks and taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there were many Muslims and Croats there, I think that they used three 10-metre long trucks and they boarded everyone who remained in the sports hall onto them. The fourth truck had a canvas tarpaulin and that truck was driven to Betonirka where there were four or five Muslims and Croats that were beaten daily. People were beaten there around the clock, all day long, all night long, every day. In addition to officers who beat them --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that you're talking about this as some background. But what I really want, if you can, is to tell me what you know happened directly with your son, Edin, at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an introduction so that you would get a clearer picture of what happened to my son. Since that was the month of July, it was terribly hot and the beating in Betonirka was around the clock. These people, some 60 people, who were totally exhausted were boarded onto one truck which was covered with a canvas tarpaulin, basically hermetically sealed, and there were perhaps a few canisters with water there. In addition to that, one of the trucks had a flat tire, so they had to spend more time in the sun, the inmates. And as they travelled to Manjaca, they died, one by one, for lack of air. Once they got to Manjaca, there were 18 dead people on that truck and 4 who still had -- showed some signs of life. Once they got to Manjaca, they got off the trucks and they started calling out the names. And as they called out the names, nobody got off that truck, so they peeked inside to see why was nobody getting off and they saw a lot of dead bodies there. They panicked and then they called for Dr. Meho Sabanovic to come urgently. The commander rushed to that spot as well. And then when the guards saw what had happened, they started yelling, "Is there anybody here with medical background who can help these people?" So my son Edin, who was in another truck and had travelled with plenty of air, volunteered, as a person with medical experience, and another man did as well. They tried to provide first aid to these people, threw water on them, gave them artificial breathing, but that didn't help much. The commander came and said, "I am not -- I will not accept any dead inmates. Take them away." So they loaded those 18 bodies onto the truck together with those four that had recovered in the meantime. And my son boarded that bus as well. They gave him a 20-litre canister of water to use it and sprinkle it on those people if they needed it. Some three or four months ago we found in Sanski Most 18 of those dead bodies, and my son's body was not there together with the body of -- bodies of other five people that got onto that truck. I don't know what happened to them. And if this Tribunal or anybody else, including Mr. Talic, can help us find them, I would be very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Any further questions, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Briefly, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, do you want a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time you need a break, let me know, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, but not right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, your third son, Nedim, he still lives and works with you in Sanski Most today. He was also taken to Manjaca. But my understanding is that he was released from there before you arrived at the end of August so that you did not see him there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you arrived here the other day, you told me that he had been able to be released and that a family connection in Banja Luka had been able to obtain his release; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, could you very briefly describe to the Chamber who this person was who had your son released and how they were able to accomplish that.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister's daughter-in-law is an engineer. She worked in a bureau in which Nino Granic worked. He was also an engineer -- a civil engineer. Nino Granic -- could you please tell me the name again -- the -- of the SAO Krajina, the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, rather than do that, let me show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Denise, this is ERN 01329897, which will be P832. There's also a draft translation which we've prepared that does not have an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise that document which you've been provided with?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document that my son gave me when I came here. He had it on him. He was keeping it. This document shows that on the 20th of June, my son was released by Vojo Kupresanin from the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think if you look up at the date, it may not be clear on the copy you have. Is not the date on the top left-hand corner the 26th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got -- on the 27th of August, and my son was released a day before I arrived there, on the 26th of August. That's -- that date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then quickly, after your son was released based on this order, he was given this document in Banja Luka for his own protection to show his status, that he had been legally -- or that he had been officially released?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were given this just before you travelled here for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My son gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now if Mr. Biscevic could be provided with the last exhibit. That's the Red Cross handover certificate, ERN 01329898.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a document which your son was given to certify his transfer from Banja Luka to Zagreb in December 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, between his -- between Nedim's release from Manjaca the day before you arrived in August 1992 and December 1992 where did he stay in Banja Luka? Where did he live during that time?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed at my sister's in Banja Luka, privately with my sister in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then after he was -- at some point after he was transferred to Zagreb, you were able to reunite with your son Nedim and with your wife and live together again.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since we have a house in Zadar, he came from Zadar and we lived -- we carried on living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then in 1995 you all returned to Sanski Most and started over again.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I -- we start with the cross-examination. When you were shown Exhibit P832, which is the document which your son Nedim got when he was released from Manjaca, you said that he -- this document shows that he was released by Vojo Kupresanin. Could you, the usher, show him the document again, please. Could you explain to the Chamber why you said that he was released by Vojo Kupresanin. I know that at the bottom -- the bottom of the page it says "Received by Vojo Kupresanin and handed over by commission composed of three persons." Do you know the events of that day when your son was actually released? Does this document mean -- this document mean that Vojo Kupresanin went there in person and took possession of your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm putting the question to you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My sister's daughter-in-law is a civil engineer, Nino Granic was my sister's director in that company, and he knew me personally because I was also involved in agriculture and he was interested in this area, so he knew me. And Vojo Kupresanin and Nino Granic are related. They have the same father or the same mother, so that Nino Granic, who was persuaded by my daughter-in-law, asked Vojo Kupresanin to release my son. That was the private connection which resulted with the release -- which resulted in the release of my son. They went to fetch my son in Manjaca. They took him away in a private car. They took him to Banja Luka. And they handed him -- they took him to my sister's house and handed him over to my sister there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You have the option of starting now but knowing that we will break in 12, 13 minutes' time or breaking now and starting immediately after the break. It's your option.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is completely the same to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can start right now and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you can start now. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if you want to clarify the answer to your own question. But the answer was: "They went to fetch my son. They took him away in a private car."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think we know who "they" are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that it was Vojo Kupresanin and Granic. That's how I understood it. If I am not understanding you well, please, sir, do tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood me well. That's what happened. Vojo Kupresanin and Granic took my son to Banja Luka in a private car and handed him over to my sister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Biscevic, I need to explain to you very briefly that according to our Rules of Procedure you now will be cross-examined by the Defence teams. The first cross-examination is that by the Defence team for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Biscevic. My name is Slobodan Zecevic. I will ask you a few questions with regard to the statement you gave or with regard to your testimony before the Trial Chamber here. Mr. Biscevic, if at any time you would like a break, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no problem. Just you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, you were the President of the Sanski Most SDA and you had a one-year term of office.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that you became a member of the executive committee of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was a member of the main board and later on I was also a member of the main board. I was a member of the main board during that term of office. As I was -- I held that capacity, I was a member of the main board and I was presiding in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you to make a pause, because we both speak the same language. So could you just provide short answers if possible, yes or no, in order to make things as short as possible, because I have an entire series of questions to put to you. So could you please pause after the question for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And that applies to you as well, Mr. Zecevic. When he finishes his answer, please don't just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Interpreter, I just said that that applies to Mr. Zecevic as well. It's important that he doesn't jump in straight away with his next question immediately after the witness has finished answering the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm completely aware of that, Your Honours. It was just the instruction to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was trying to be helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, given that you carried out these responsibilities within the SDA party in Sanski Most. You are certainly aware of the fact -- the international [As translated] situation was deteriorating in the -- in the 1990s in the town.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I became the president, the relations between the three peoples, the Croats, the Muslims, and the Serbs, there were no problems. Everything was quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You became president immediately after the elections in 1990; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means up until August 1991 there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in the course of 1991, you could already see that there were certain problems.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this inter-ethnic situation, it was deteriorating throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina as a result of the overall situation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us on page 53 of the unofficial transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Judge Taya has brought my attention to what appears in the transcript -- the international situation was deteriorating. You said the inter-ethnical. So for the record, it should be inter-ethnic situation and not international situation. Thank you. Thank you, Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday while you were giving your testimony you told us that the war which started in Croatia in 1991 made the situation worse to a large extent.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, because at the beginning when they were calling up reserve forces, Rasula Nedeljko and Tunic Ante we went to calm the soldiers down because the Muslims and the Croats refused to respond to those call-up papers. They didn't want to go to Croatia from Sanski Most. So we tried there to sort this out. We went with official vehicles. We went to visit the soldiers, and we spoke to them. This is what happened at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, in -- when you were giving your testimony yesterday you said that the position of the SDA party was that reservists, even if they had been called to join the army, the position was that they shouldn't respond to those call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time that was contrary to the regulations which were in force.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the regulations of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something. We are assuming that these are the federal regulations of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA sent the call-up papers, not the Yugoslav state. The Yugoslav People's Army sent out these call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I remind you again, sir, to allow a pause after Mr. Zecevic finishes his question, because you are jumping in -- you are anticipating the rest of the question. You start answering it even before he's finished the question. And that's causing a lot of problems to the interpreters. They are giving me signs from everywhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "the regulations," I'm referring to the laws in the sense that not responding to call-up papers was a crime in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me -- yesterday you told us in the course of your testimony on page 58, line 22 to 25 you said that not only -- not only was the SDA's position that soldiers should not respond to the call-up but you said that you even prohibited people from responding to these call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after that a certain decision was found, according to which those people who failed to respond and did so voluntarily -- those people who did not respond to the call-up papers, they were told that they had to return uniforms and all weapons that had been issued to them.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a plan of the JNA. They didn't say by accident that they should surrender their weapons and their uniforms. This was not done accidentally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify one matter. The people I'm talking about received call-up papers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They consciously refused to respond to those call-up papers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They refused to respond to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Although in their military booklets -- according to their military booklets they were members, official members, of the reserve forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Given that they did so quite consciously, the army instead of initiating proceedings against them simply decided to order them to return their weapons -- to return their uniforms and the weapons that had been issued to them.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The call-up papers that members of the Muslim people got had been in the JNA. But in such a case they went to Croatia. They were on the front line. And they would be returned to the Sanski Most in boxes. That's why we said, "Don't respond to the call-up. But if necessary be in Sanski Most and if necessary protect your homes. Don't worry about Yugoslavia." You know what the situation was in Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991, that's right. We have six or seven -- you can see that at the cemetery -- people who died in the JNA at the time, and they were not to blame for anything. It's just because they had ugly names. They were shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop here, Mr. Zecevic. We'll continue at 5.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I recognise Mr. Koumjian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very quickly, Your Honour, I just want to convey a scheduling request from Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: She wanted to know if it's possible for this court to switch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To sit on Saturday? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Monday morning instead of Monday afternoon. The -- and switch with Judge -- with the Stakic case. And Judge Schomburg indicated that that Trial Chamber had no problem with it. The reason being, her plan would be to have the witness, Mr. McLeod, finish his testimony here on Monday morning in this trial and then start testifying in Stakic in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday is what -- the 21st is Friday. No? The 24th. The 24th. The 24th we're sitting in the afternoon. And you -- Stakic is sitting in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And her request would be to switch, if that's agreeable with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's check with the Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately we explained to our learned colleagues that this is not acceptable for us, because I myself and my colleague Ms. Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau, we have some private things to attend and -- which were planned before in advance for Monday morning. So unfortunately we really cannot. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if they're not going to be here, it doesn't make much sense for me to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suppose you have your answer, Mr. Koumjian. And I think the witness has to testify first in -- in Stakic, as I see it, then continue here. Or else --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I mean, just convey the message to Ms. Korner and then -- I'm sure that you'll find a way. Either we -- if at all. I mean, we won't start with his evidence on Friday. I don't know. I mean, perhaps you can make an arrangement with Judge Schomburg in Stakic to start on Friday, perhaps rather than on Monday having finished -- we could do that. I don't know. Now, Mr. Biscevic, you are a professional man and I am sure you are pretty much -- you are highly intelligent. I can notice that. And being highly intelligent, you would have noticed straight away that I decided to go to a break when I did because I was sensing that you were reacting in a way to the series of questions that Mr. Zecevic was putting to you which was likely to lead you -- you and him into a head-on collision. I know that you are going to understand me perfectly well in what I'm going to tell you. Mr. Zecevic here, like all the other Defence lawyer, have got a duty to accomplish here. Their duty is to defend their clients. Their duty also is to help this Trial Chamber in its search for the truth. But in doing that, they have a duty towards their client. In the course of their cross-examination, I am sure that there will be moments when they will put questions to you which will not render your role here as a witness or your testimony any easier than you would have expected it to be. I am sure that you will understand that we cannot allow a situation to obtain in which you start arguing or raising your voice -- neither you or him, nor anyone else. No one is going to be allowed to do that. But please try to understand that they are doing their duty and they have an interest to defend their clients. And when they put a question to you, try to answer that question in a -- in a -- a civilised way, as I am sure you as a professional are -- you are trained to do. With that, Mr. Zecevic, please continue. And I also appeal to you to be considerate in the questions that you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Of course I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biscevic, we left it off at a point where you mentioned to us that six to seven people who were killed and buried were killed while they were members of the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know these people?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some names, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pasakada. He was an active officer in the JNA. He was buried in Sanski Most, and his mother when she asked her Serb neighbours while Sanski Most was liberated where were you escaping, she got a bullet in her forehead. She was killed by the officers of that same JNA. This is how they expressed their gratitude to her. And if you wish, I can take you to the cemetery to see what it says on her tombstone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, I simply asked you to give us some names if you remembered them.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told you. Pasakada was the mother's name. I forgot this young man's name. I had many patients, and I cannot remember all of their names, but he's buried in Sanski Most on the cemetery there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this was an active officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we are not talking about reservists here.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We're talking about active soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So other than this one active officer, you cannot remember any other names?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you insist, I can get the names for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, you probably know that everything that had to do with recruitment, mobilisation, and other personal matters of reservists and conscripts was done by the municipal secretariats of national defence all over the former Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that these municipal secretariats existed within municipalities; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me -- there were such fellow citizens of yours who responded to call-up papers, to mobilisation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And they would come back home from the front and bring with them a part of that war atmosphere; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serb army wasn't interested in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to please answer my question. I asked you the following: When these people came back home for their leave, when they came home from the front, they would bring with them a part of that war atmosphere. They would bring it back to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they would come home, take a bath, take a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that these people would come back, bring weapons from the front with them, and they would get drunk and cavort in Sanski Most; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was typical. Most of them did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that that led to some incidents in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that the police in Sanski Most investigated these incidents but failed to find the perpetrators as a result of which you proposed that joint patrols be established.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning. After that the army felt very strong and neglected everybody else, ignored everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We are now referring to 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, Mr. Biscevic, isn't it true that the SDA organised on its own initiative a -- patrols of single ethnicity that patrolled Mahala, the Muslim neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Muslim neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please. Mahala is a part of Sanski Most, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These patrols consisting of only one ethnicity, were members of these patrols also members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But they were all Muslims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, since this was a purely Muslim neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were these patrols armed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, in that period of time all the way until the end of 1991 the police in Sanski Most wasn't of a single ethnicity, was it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until the end of May, it was a mixed police force. And thereafter it was a Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So until May 1992 there was mixed police in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ratio was 80:15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, you had meetings then at the city level and the municipal level trying to came down the situation and prevent it from escalating.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't succeed much, did you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that it was mostly non-Serb property that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a hundred per cent so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on April 14, 1992 a bomb was thrown on a Serb cafe?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it was done by Serbs. It was done by the son of Lazic Mico. He was not a loyal Serb, so Serbs did this to him in order to make him loyal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But at any rate, the Serb property was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was proven later who was behind this, who threw the bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was that established by the police, what you're telling us now, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By us, politicians. And when we were in a meeting, we told them, "Well, look what had happened."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Please allow a pause. Because again you're jumping in straight away with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me, was there a proceeding instigated as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked that that be done, but there was no result. We were not able to establish who was to blame for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in this particular case, when a bomb had been thrown on a cafe owned by a Serb, you, the politicians, knew who was the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because they had an argument among themselves, and then they revealed who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you reported that to the police but nothing was done about it.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once they found out who was the perpetrator, nothing was done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And all other incidents in which Croat and Muslim property was damaged, even you politicians didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we knew everything, but there was nothing we could do. We knew that Medini and Njunja went through the town every night. That they were doing whatever they wanted. We knew that, but there was nothing we could do. All of our talk was in vain, because people saw him at night walking around and throwing bombs. My son personally saw the white Mercedes from which a bomb was launched, but nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about, is whether these facts that you are revealing here today were available to the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing done about it. It was no use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the police that was in charge of maintaining law and order in Sanski Most did nothing regarding these incidents.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they considered that something ought to be done, then they did their job perfectly well. In the other cases, they did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a person called Njunja. You probably know of a paramilitary formation of which he was a commander, the SOS.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SOS was established in Sanski Most later on, and Njunja was the president of it. And later on a bomb was put under his vehicle, under his car, and he was blown together with the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the issue of mobilisation. Since the position was that the Muslims did not respond to call-up papers, which was against the mandatory legal regulations, that at the same time meant that they did not become members of the Territorial Defence because they failed to respond to these call-up papers as well.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we said loud and clear that if the call-up papers was for the municipality of Sanski Most, then it was okay to respond. However, if it was for the front in Croatia, then it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Out of these people who consciously failed to respond to call-up papers, they had to surrender their weapons and uniforms; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had to return the weapons and uniforms they had been issued with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these weapons, as you told us, were stored in the Sanski Most SUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a military office in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this storing of weapons -- of returned weapons started in 1991, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1992. Not in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, please, was this warehouse secured by the police? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the son of Mico Lazic came to see me, the one whose cafe was bombed, because he had not been active from the very beginning. He came in a truck to my house and he confiscated the weapons from the neighbourhood and he took it to the military office. We did not receive any kind of receipt or any kind of explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about your civilian weapons that you had. I was talking about the weapons that was seized from the military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they had to turn it to the military over and a record was made of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that those weapons were stored in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two buildings, one was the Territorial Defence and one was SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to remind you every -- every five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't let him finish his question. So Mr. Zecevic, please repeat your question, and then I'm sure Mr. Biscevic will allow the pause that I have been recommending and answered. Your question had --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that these -- that those weapons were stored in the SUP. And you were stopped there by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what you were going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Presumably, because earlier on you have put a question whether it was secured by the police -- whether the warehouse was secured by the police or not, whether the witness knew. And he answered you -- gave you an answer which has nothing to do exactly with the question which you -- which you had put.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me -- Mr. Biscevic, we need to clarify this. These weapons were stored in the SUP building, and that building was shared by the SUP and the municipal Secretariat for People's Defence. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this satisfy the requirement by the Honourable Trial Chamber because your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. But again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer, let him finish. Make sure that there is enough -- sufficient interval of time so that the -- because I don't understand your language and the other two Judges don't understand your language and the Prosecutors don't understand your language. So we have to wait for the interpreters -- not to mention Mr. Ackerman, who doesn't also understand the language. So we have to wait until there is a translation, an interpretation, which sometimes isn't finished when you have already started answering the question. This is why I'm stopping you every -- every so often, because otherwise we -- it creates problems for everyone. Yes. But he did answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biscevic, the municipal Secretariat for National Defence is a civilian body, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "at the beginning," what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the 6th Krajina Brigade came to Sanski Most, Mr. Basara took everything into his hands. The Territorial Defence, led by a Serb for many years, was given to us, to the Muslims a few months prior to that, and that Muslim who headed the Territorial Defence ended up in Manjaca. So you can see how much power he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So according to you, all the way until the 6th Krajina Brigade came, that was a civilian body; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was the state of war ever proclaimed in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the 6th Krajina Brigade came, was the state of war proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said then that the army was the guarantor of peace between Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, that we politicians can bicker all we want but that the army came in as a guarantor of peace and would not allow any harm to happen to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday on page 56 of the unofficial transcript, line 2 and 3, that you met Colonel Basara when he came to Sanski Most together with the 6th Krajina Brigade and that was sometime in March of 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when Mr. Basara came to a meeting in the municipality and he said that he had come with his army to take a rest there and to get acquainted with us and promised that we would be in constant contact and we would solve all the problems that arose, that we politicians could do what we wanted but that the army would be the guarantor of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the document P608, 608.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biscevic, I'm about to show you a document which is an order of the 5th Corps command dated April 1, 1992. Did you take a look at it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't get a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you start reading, please, item 2, which starts with the words "After the march." That's item one. Could you please read that for us.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "After the march deploy the unit in Sanski Most Kamengrad village, Dabar village, Tomina village. The area with the following tasks, achieving full control of the territory, preventing inter-ethnic conflicts, setting up road blocks, and securing features of special importance. Establish full cooperation with the organs of government in Sanski Most municipality and collaboration with TO and police units."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please now can you take a look at the second page. It says that -- it was signed by Momir Talic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see on this document that it is dated April 1, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Judge Janu is rightly pointing out. You did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pose the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, because there is another document which is only similar. I will pose the documents afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Afterwards -- afterwards, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biscevic, you will see that this is a regular combat report issued by the 5th Corps command to the 2nd military district command on the 2nd of April, 1992. I would ask you to read the second paragraph under item 1 [As interpreted], please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the day the 6/10 of the -- the 6th Brigade of the 10th Partisan Division has been withdrawn from combat in the Demirovac village, Draksenic village, Josik village area with the aim of preparing and forcing a march during the night of 2nd/3rd April 1992 along the Josik village, Bosanska Dubica village, Prijedor Ostra Luka village, Sanski Most axis and the area of Kamengrad village, Dabar village, Sanski Most Tomina village by 0600 hours on 3rd April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the paragraph that you wanted him to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because according to the transcript it says the second paragraph of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 2, I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the transcript -- we'll correct that, at least for the record. Because your question was: I would ask you to read the second paragraph under item 1, please. And he has not read the second paragraph under item 1 presumably because what he read was what you asked him to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. He understood exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But for the record we must put it that it's not the paragraph that was put in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, now, could you please read out first paragraph under item 3 in the same document. That's page 3. It starts with the words "I decided."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the next page, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian version, it's the page number 3. And the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's further down. Usher, it's there. There. We are getting to it. Stop there, please. "I have decided by pulling the --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I have decided by pulling the 6/10 part unit out of combat to establish complete control over the broader Sanski Most area and use other forces grouped in the zone of responsibility south of the Sava River to prevent the mounting of barricades on the roads, thus ensuring free flow of traffic, protection of the population, and prevention of inter-ethnic conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you don't want me to read any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Signed by Commander Major General Momir Talic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, you saw the dates on these documents.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It indicates -- they indicate that the 6th Krajina Brigade came to Sanski Most on the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that it was indeed in the beginning of April, not in March, as you said?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this because in your statement given to the investigators of the OTP on two occasions in 1997 and two occasions in 1999 you said somewhere in those statements that it was even in January or February 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have said January or February. I might have said March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But at any rate, we agreed that it was most probably on the 3rd of April, 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have established that it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please. These orders, these two documents that you just took a look at and the document that's in front of you right now, are fully in accord with what was told to you by Colonel Basara at one of the meetings when you met him and when he came to a meeting in the municipality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Biscevic, the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina from let's say the beginning of April onwards deteriorated terribly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There were armed conflicts in Sarajevo in the beginning of April in Sarajevo and then in other places in Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that time operations in Croatia and in Western Slavonia were still ongoing and geographically this area is quite close to you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- let's return to Sanski Most. According to our information, the MUP and the events in the municipality building took place on the 17th of April, 1992. Yesterday you said that it was the 25th or the 26th of April, that it was on those dates. Could you tell us whether it was on the 25th, the 26th, and the 27th or the 17th, 18th, and 19th, if you can remember this.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1992. And now it's 2002. So I may have got the dates wrong. That's possible. But it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day, when the MUP was divided, you entered the municipality building; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the SDA leadership, members of the HDZ leadership from Sanski Most also entered the municipality building; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the municipality building was also entered by these policemen who weren't members of -- who weren't of Serbian nationality. They also entered the building together with you.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they were forcibly expelled from the SUP, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, some civilians also entered the building. You said that too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were there in the municipality building, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there that evening. I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the course of that period of time, March/April 1992, were there any negotiations between the SDS an SDA leadership so the SDS and the SDA parties, about the division of the Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right up until the attack on the municipal assembly we would try to agree every day and we would discuss all current issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you specifically talk about dividing the Sanski Most municipality along ethnic demarcation lines? Do you remember such a thing?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS made such a request. There was nothing else we could do but sit down and discuss this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA party didn't agree with such a proposal.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the municipality building the members of the police were armed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one of them had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that on the 19th of April - you didn't say that date exactly, you said the 27th - but it was on that day you said that you left the municipality building and went to your farm. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that you didn't return to the municipality building, did you, that evening?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Checkpoints had just been set up, and it was impossible to enter that area because soldiers were there and they were manning the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you subsequently heard that about 2200 hours some sort of projectile had been fired at the municipality building; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably a sign for a general shooting, because they started shooting from all sorts of weapons all over Sanski Most at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to that event, did you perhaps hear some sort of exchange of fire? So I mean just before that projectile was fired, if you can remember that.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well. That wasn't unusual for us. They were shooting everywhere, all over the place, because people were half drunk and they had as many bullets as they wanted, they could shoot as much as they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since as you say you were not there, did anyone tell you that prior to the projectile being fired, there was a conflict between the police standing in front of the municipality building and certain people who were in the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether given that you weren't there, as you said, did someone tell you or did you hear from someone that immediately prior to the projectile being fired there was an armed conflict between the police forces standing in front of the building and, let's say, the people who were in the building, in the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just asked you whether you had heard anything about that. Thank you. On that day, as you said you were on your farm; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But yesterday you told us that after the SDA leadership had left the municipality building, you said that you went to sleep -- to spend the night in the village of Sehovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I, but the people who were in the municipality building. At the time I was referring to the SDA and HDZ parties, the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you personally were not in Sehovci.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. At the time, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, General Talic arrived by helicopter and you didn't attend that meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But as far as you were told - and you spoke about this yesterday - he repeated what we just read a minute ago in the order and what Colonel Basara told you at the beginning of April; isn't that correct? That the --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also claimed that the JNA was a guarantor of peace in Sanski Most, that they would guarantee the peace between the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats. He said that he stood by this claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to raise a matter and requires about five minutes or a little more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have an entire five or six minutes. Whatever. But I want to accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you to stop, then stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I actually have one more question on this subject, and then I'm moving to something else. So it would be a perfect place to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Mr. Karabeg two days after that meeting with General Talic he spoke to him one more time over the phone?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you what they discussed, if you can remember? Or perhaps it was the same matter.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that Mr. Talic had guaranteed peace and security, that the attack against Sana was a mistake and he said that it wouldn't be repeated. He said that the situation in the municipality of Sanski Most would be calm. He said there would be no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Biscevic, we have to stop here today and we will continue tomorrow. You will be escorted now again like you were yesterday by the usher. Tomorrow we will resume at 9.00 in the morning, not in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow we will resume at 9.00 in the morning, not in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour must quail with horror at seeing me appear. But it's the question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not me. Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness Charles McLeod. I know it's been raised. I saw -- I was sent an e-mail but I don't think the problems are quite perhaps clear. Your Honour will recall that Mr. McLeod is a businessman we've had some difficulty in getting here. He made time for the three days, the Friday, the Monday, and the Tuesday. He has to be back -- he has to finish on Tuesday because he's got a presentation in connection with his business on the Wednesday in Glasgow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The unexpected problem that arose today for the first time was that Stakic next week -- it does alternate fortnights apparently is sitting in the morning and not sitting full sessions. On Monday it's only sitting from 10.00 until quarter to 2.00. And Tuesday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Monday is from 10.00 ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Until quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it loses an hour. And on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's sitting between 9.00 and quarter to 1.00, losing another hour. Mr. McLeod as I understand it -- and it may well be in any event that tomorrow's witnesses may go into Friday. Although I have no doubt that he will be short in chief, from what I understood Mr. Ackerman had to say, he may be -- they don't want to be time constrained, and I understand that. The difficulty is, if he's not finished on Friday in this court he can't obviously start his evidence in Stakic in the middle of his evidence here, which is why Judge Schomburg, when the problem was put, said if it was agreeable to this court he would swap the sessions and that way it would -- it would work and they could sit a full session indeed on Monday. I understand that the reason given that Mr. Ackerman doesn't object but that counsel for Mr. -- for General Talic do. And I just wondered if it was purely personal, whether the interests of the Court might not perhaps override it on this occasion. It really will be very difficult to get him back here for further cross-examination if necessary, so that's -- I'm appealing effectively to the good nature of counsel. If it's only personal as opposed to professional, in other words, they have professional reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. And I will not ask counsel to explain --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely not. But however, perhaps Mr. Zecevic or Madam Fauveau would like -- if you could perhaps meet -- meet Ms. Korner halfway, I don't know. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would very much like to -- to help the Prosecutor and this Court as well, but believe me, I don't have any alternative in this respect. That is why I adamantly said that this is not acceptable for me. Because as you know, I jumped into this so to speak trial after only 14 days, and there is so many things that I actually didn't finish but I -- I really would like to -- this is one thing that I cannot postpone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a personal matter, and -- I mean, if my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- Ms. Fauveau would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber doesn't want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I'm just trying to be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two counsel. That's what I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Madam Fauveau, if it's purely personal --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But my problem is of a professional nature. As Ms. Korner knows, I work in a -- for an office in Paris and I have certain professional engagements over there. It will be very difficult to accommodate such last-minute changes. It would be very difficult for me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I -- perhaps I hoped too much that there might be some meeting here, when it really is a matter of the interests of the court. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod is arriving when?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod is arriving tomorrow evening, quite late on because of his professional commitments. I will call him on Friday. I don't know whether there's a possibility perhaps of starting on Friday a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I even offered to start in the morning if you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The trouble is I need to -- I won't have seen him at all. I can see him quite early. If Your Honours were able to sit perhaps part of the morning and then the rest of the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- I'd be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could do that, if that doesn't cause a problem to the Defence. It's -- because the thing you have to understand, that I am prepared and we are prepared to accommodate each and every one of you, but everyone has rights. So the moment anyone from the Defence says no, we -- we can't meet --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well -- but, Your Honour, I tell you what. I don't think I need a great deal of time to speak to Mr. McLeod. It's effectively just a question of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Because if you could do that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could perhaps start on Friday at -- because in any event, I anticipate -- because I see Mr. Biscevic is still being cross-examined -- there are two witnesses coming tomorrow that Ms. Richterova is going to call. I anticipate they'll still need to be finishing on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Friday. That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So if Your Honour -- exactly. And then I can start Mr. McLeod at around 12.00 midday or whatever time ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically let's start from here. You have -- after Mr. Biscevic's testimony, you have two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two -- yes, relatively short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I was given to understand earlier on today that some wishful thinking has suggested that there is a possibility of finishing with both of them tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- that really was wishful thinking, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
